newsitem.title: USA: Clinton has little time to savor re-election.
newsitem.headline: Clinton has little time to savor re-election.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Wednesday prepared for a triumphal return to Washington where Cabinet changes, potential scandals and foreign policy challenges gave him little time to savor his sweeping re-election.

Republicans who hung on to control of Congress promised to work with Clinton on his legislative priorities but also vowed to look into irregularities in Democratic campaign fund-raising, among other alleged ethical abuses.

A welcome-home party was planned at the White House for Clinton's return from Little Rock, Arkansas, where he celebrated the election returns on Tuesday night and appealed to Republicans in his victory speech to "put aside the politics of division and build America's community together."
With 98 percent of the vote counted, Clinton had about 50 percent to 41 percent for Republican Bob Dole and nine percent for third-party candidate Ross Perot.

At the top of Clinton's agenda was a transition to a second four-year term that aides said would include a Cabinet shuffle and the departure of some senior staff including Secretary of State Warren Christopher. Defence officials say Secretary William Perry has also told Clinton he wants to leave the Pentagon, possibly within a few months.

Officials insist there is no deadline for Clinton to act since his second term does not start until January, but they indicated he would like to announce some decisions before he departs on Tuesday on a lengthy trip that includes a vacation in Hawaii and visits to the Philippines, Australia and Thailand.

Christopher's resignation, expected to be announced soon, comes at a time of difficult foreign policy challenges such as Russian relations in the wake of President Boris Yeltin's heart bypass surgery.

In addition, the president faces problems in the U.S. withdrawal of troops from Bosnia and in pursuing Middle East peace. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu signalled a hard line, telling Arabs not to expect Clinton to pressure Israel into making peace concessions.
Congratulations from London, Beijing and other major capitals poured in while stock prices rose on world markets on news that Clinton had won but Republicans would continue to control Congress.

But hanging over Clinton are Republican pledges to search for administration scandals. Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi said there would soon be a new set of investigative hearings on Capitol Hill looking into questions about how Clinton's Democratic Party had raised funds.

Lott said Republicans were particularly interested in John Huang, a former Commerce Department official said to have raised hundreds of thousands of dollars from Asian business interests and Asian Americans for the Democratic Party.

Representative Dan Burton, a conservative Indiana Republican poised to chair the House Government Reform and Oversight Committee, pledged to be "thorough and uncompromising" but added: "At the same time, I will be fair and responsible. There will be no witch hunts."
But Democratic Party general chairman Sen. Christopher Dodd of Connecticut said the fact that Clinton won should be seen as a sign Americans were fed up with such investigations.

"We've got to stop the backbiting. I hope these investigations, subpoenas, this stuff will end. I'm telling you, people are sick of it in this country. They want to see people work together," he told CNN.

There has been speculation from White House Chief of Staff Leon Panetta and other top officials that Clinton might try to put some Republicans into his Cabinet to provide balance. This would doubtless be seen as an effort to blunt the opposition.

Clinton on Tuesday became the first Democrat to win re-election to the White House since Franklin Roosevelt in 1944. He won almost 50 percent of the popular vote, carrying 31 states and the District of Columbia for 379 Electoral College votes, far more than the 270 needed for victory. Dole won 19 states for 159 electoral votes.

Dole, the 73-year-old Second World War hero whose "one last mission" ended in a nose dive, was headed to his vacation home in Bal Harbour, Florida, for rest and reflection on why it all went so badly.

He is often mentioned as a candidate for a special commission Clinton is expected to appoint to examine how to reform Medicare and Social Security, two entitlement programmes whose costs are contributing heavily to the budget deficit.

Clinton aides were quick to claim that the president -- denigrated by Republicans for having won in 1992 with only 43 percent of the vote -- had won a strong mandate for governing by receiving about 50 percent of the vote.

The Democrats fell short of the 19 seats they needed to take back control of the 435-seat House of Representatives , but the reduced Republican majority could give moderates more influence. Speaker Newt Gingrich, who is certain to remain in the job despite being blamed for creating the conditions that led to Clinton's revival, pledged to reach out to Clinton.

"I think we ought to work with him, give him a chance to lead in the direction he campaigned on. And if he sticks with the things he campaigned on we should to be able to find some common ground to actually pass some things that are good for America early in 1997," Gingrich said.
